counterevidence: List prices, not what contracted buyers pay; spot and reserved prices diverge from on-demand; one aggregator, and its panel of providers changes week to week; an older chip's rent falls as newer chips arrive, with no glut.
definition: Weekly median on-demand rental price per H100 GPU-hour across the cloud providers GetDeploying tracks; H200 and B200 alongside.

direction_rule.rationale: Four weekly readings, a month. A move of fifteen cents an hour or less is noise in a median across some forty providers whose panel changes week to week; rising rents mean the owners of GPUs keep more of the value.

name: GPU rental price per hour

status_events.author: claude
status_events.counterevidence_considered: List prices, not contracted prices; reserved and spot prices sit well below on-demand, so a glut could show there first.
status_events.reason: First reading, from GetDeploying's weekly median of on-demand list prices across the cloud providers it tracks. An H100 rented for $3.21 an hour in the week of 21 Sep 2026, against $3.20 four weeks before (inside the fifteen-cent dead band, so stable) and $2.95 a year before (up about 9%). One aggregator at tier 3 caps the status at emerging.

timing_rationale: Leading: rental prices fall as capacity outruns demand, ahead of neocloud earnings.
tracker_interpretation: The H100's median rent fell by about a sixth into the spring and has since climbed back above where it stood a year before; newer chips rent for more. No sign of the glut that follows an overbuild.
why_it_matters: The cloud layer's price per unit of compute; falling rental prices are the neoclouds' rent eroding, and a crash would be the glut that bandwidth went through in 2001.
